title: What astronauts do
keyIdea: Astronauts are people who travel to space in rockets. Space starts about 100 km above the ground, far above where planes fly, and there is no air to breathe there, so astronauts wear a spacesuit with a helmet and an air backpack. Today astronauts live and work for months on the International Space Station, about 400 km up, where everything floats: they drink from pouches, sleep in bags tied to the wall and exercise every day. In 1969 Neil Armstrong was the first person to walk on the Moon, and 12 people walked there by 1972.
familyTip: Fill a cup and a bottle with a sports cap, then tip each one over a sink: which would work on the space station, where water floats out in balls? On a clear evening, look up the space station's pass times for your town on NASA's Spot the Station site and watch it glide over as a bright moving dot.

visual.caption: Used by astronauts in space, or not? Drag each card, or tap it and then tap a box.

items: A drink pouch with a straw
A sleeping bag tied to the wall
A sun hat instead of a helmet

lab.caption: Flagship lab: suit up an astronaut, fly a rocket up to the space station, drink, sleep, eat and keep fit where things float, jump on the Moon, check a robot.

kid: An astronaut is a person who goes to space. A big rocket takes them up. Space starts about 100 km above us. Planes fly much lower, about 10 km up.
There is no air in space. So astronauts wear a spacesuit. The helmet and the backpack give them air to breathe. Gloves and boots keep out the heat and the cold.

Today astronauts live on the space station. It goes round the Earth about 16 times a day. Up there, things float. Astronauts drink from a pouch with a straw. They sleep in a bag tied to the wall. They exercise every day to keep their bones strong.
Long ago, astronauts went to the Moon. In 1969 Neil Armstrong was the first person to walk on it. The Moon pulls less than the Earth, so they could jump much higher.
adult: Ages 5 to 7. This topic gives the human side of space before children study rovers and the history of space exploration. Key words: astronaut, rocket, spacesuit, helmet, oxygen, International Space Station (ISS), orbit, float, gravity, the Moon, Apollo.

Facts to know (NASA): space is usually said to start about 100 km up. Airliners cruise about 10 to 12 km up. The ISS orbits about 400 km up and goes round about 16 times a day. People have lived on it since November 2000, each crew for about six months. Crews exercise about two hours a day, because bones and muscles weaken when they carry no weight. They sleep in bags fixed to the wall, drink from pouches and eat tortillas, since bread crumbs float into eyes and kit. Apollo 11 landed on 20 July 1969. Neil Armstrong and then Buzz Aldrin walked on the Moon, and 12 people did so by the end of 1972.

A common mistake is to think there is no gravity on the space station. At 400 km up, gravity is still about 90% as strong as on the ground. Things float because the station and all in it fall round the Earth together. Children also often think astronauts live on the Moon now, or that a hat or goggles would do in space. The suit is needed because there is no air. On the Moon gravity is about one sixth of Earth's, so the same jump goes about six times as high.

In the lab your child picks the four suit parts that keep an astronaut alive, drags a rocket to where planes fly, where space starts and to the space station, chooses how astronauts drink, sleep, eat and keep fit, compares a jump on Earth with one on the Moon, and checks a robot's sayings.

practice.prompt: There are {a} astronauts on the space station. A rocket brings {b} more. How many astronauts are on the station now?
practice.hint: Start at {a} and count on {b} more.
practice.explain: {a} and {b} more make {=a+b} astronauts. Crews come and go by rocket, so the number changes.

practice.prompt: An astronaut exercises for 2 hours every day. How many hours is that in {a} days?
practice.hint: Count in twos, one 2 for each day.
practice.explain: {a} lots of 2 hours is {=2*a} hours. Exercise every day keeps bones and muscles strong while things float.

practice.prompt: Why does an astronaut wear a helmet outside the space station?
choices: There is no air to breathe in space
To keep the rain off
Space is very windy
practice.hint: Think about what we breathe, and whether space has any.
practice.explain: Space has no air. The helmet and the air backpack give the astronaut air to breathe.

practice.prompt: How do astronauts drink on the space station?
choices: From a pouch with a straw
From an open cup
From a tap into a glass
practice.hint: Water floats out of an open cup up there.
practice.explain: Water floats out of a cup in wobbly balls, so astronauts drink from a closed pouch with a straw.

practice.prompt: Which is highest above the ground?
choices: The space station
A plane
A tall building
practice.hint: Planes fly about 10 km up. Space starts about 100 km up.
practice.explain: The space station is about 400 km up, far above planes at about 10 km and buildings even lower.

pool.prompt: On Earth an astronaut jumps {a} cm high. On the Moon the same jump goes about 6 times as high. About how many cm is that?
pool.hint: Add {a} cm six times, or count in {a}s six times.
pool.explain: 6 lots of {a} cm is {=6*a} cm. The Moon pulls you less, so you go higher.

pool.prompt: The space station goes round the Earth {a} times in the morning and {b} times in the afternoon. How many times is that?
pool.hint: Add the morning trips and the afternoon trips.
pool.explain: {a} and {b} make {=a+b} trips round the Earth. It goes round about once every hour and a half.

pool.prompt: Who was the first person to walk on the Moon?
choices: Neil Armstrong, in 1969
Nobody has ever walked on the Moon
An astronaut who lives there now
pool.hint: It happened a long time ago, in 1969.
pool.explain: Neil Armstrong stepped onto the Moon on 20 July 1969. Nobody lives on the Moon.

pool.prompt: Where do astronauts live and work today?
choices: On the space station, going round the Earth
In houses on the Moon
On the Sun
pool.hint: It goes round and round the Earth.
pool.explain: Astronauts live for months on the International Space Station. No one lives on the Moon.

pool.prompt: How do astronauts sleep on the space station?
choices: In a sleeping bag tied to the wall
On a bed with a pillow
Floating loose round the room
pool.hint: Everything floats, so it has to be tied on.
pool.explain: Things float there, so the sleeping bag is tied to the wall and the astronaut does not drift into anything.

pool.prompt: Why do astronauts eat tortilla wraps instead of bread?
choices: Bread crumbs would float into eyes and machines
Bread is too heavy for a rocket
There are no shops in space
pool.hint: Think about what happens to crumbs where things float.
pool.explain: Crumbs do not fall to the floor in space. They float about, so wraps that make almost no crumbs are safer.

pool.prompt: Things float on the space station. Is there gravity there?
choices: Yes, they float because the station is falling round the Earth
No, there is no gravity in space
No, gravity stops at the clouds
pool.hint: Gravity keeps the station going round the Earth.
pool.explain: Gravity is still there. The station and everything in it fall round the Earth together, so things float.

pool.prompt: Why does an astronaut need to exercise every day in space?
choices: To keep bones and muscles strong
To stop floating away
To make the rocket go faster
pool.hint: Floating means the body does not have to hold itself up.
pool.explain: Floating makes bones and muscles weak. About 2 hours of exercise a day keeps them strong.
